The paragraph states 1.10pt.

This article preliminarily characterizes political fake news on Twitter using meta-data from more than 1.5M tweets collected on Donald Trump's election day, focusing on viral tweets, exposure, accounts, polarization, followers, URLs, and verification.
The paragraph contains ].

Fake news became mainstream in politics during the 2016 United States presidential election, prompting governments and corporations including Google BIBREF1 and Facebook BIBREF2 to address its effects, though definition, identification, and stopping remain limited.

Since the Obama campaign in 2008, social media has been pervasive in United States politics, with up to 62% of American adults receiving news from social media BIBREF4, facilitating fake news diffusion through limited filtering, fact-checking, or editorial judgement.

Craig Silverman BIBREF5 confirmed the rise of fake news, stating that top-performing fake election news stories on Facebook generated more engagement than top stories from major news outlets in the final three months of the US presidential campaign.

The research assumes social media is a conduit for fake news and uses more that 1.5M tweets collected on November 8th 2016 to identify features of tweets containing fake news through meta-data, following Morris et al. BIBREF6.

The goals are to compare tweets labelled as containing fake news with tweets labelled as not containing them, characterize viral fake-news tweets and originating accounts through meta-data, and determine political polarization.
The study uses number of retweets to identify viral tweets, defines fake news using Rubin et al. BIBREF7 categories, and uses a manually labelled, publicly released dataset BIBREF8.
The paragraph introduces main observations from the results.

The findings resonate with Allcot and Gentzkow BIBREF9, provide external validity to previous research, stress meta-data's importance, and underscore parameters useful for identifying fake news on Twitter.
The rest of the paper discusses the literature and fake news type, presents hypotheses, data, and methodology, then presents findings, conclusions, and future lines of work.

A survey by Conroy and colleagues BIBREF10 identifies linguistic approaches using text, linguistic characteristics, and machine learning, and network approaches using network characteristics and meta-data, to single-out fake news.

Psychology, political science, and sociology studies BIBREF11, BIBREF12, BIBREF13, BIBREF14 examine misinformation belief and report that priming effects and confirmation bias affect people's ability to discern misinformation.

An Economics paper BIBREF9 found fake news sites often resemble legitimate organizations, tend to be short-lived, are more likely shared than legitimate articles from trusted sources, and exhibit larger polarization.
Because defining fake news is unresolved, the work relies on Rubin et al. BIBREF7 categorization and introduces five categories with illustrative examples from the dataset.
Previous works suggest important determinants for adoption and diffusion of fake news, and the hypotheses identify three dimensions that may help distinguish fake news from legit information.
Taking three dimensions into account, the authors propose hypotheses about features that may identify tweets containing fake news, to be tested over the collected dataset.
The paragraph states Exposure.
The paragraph states Characterization.
The paragraph states Polarization.

Public tweets were collected using Twitter's public API and the filter endpoint of the streaming API on Nov 8th 2016 with #MyVote2016, #ElectionDay, #electionnight, @realDonaldTrump, and @HillaryClinton.
The study characterizes viral tweets containing fake news, defines a tweet as viral if retweeted more than 1000 times, and cites Body et al. BIBREF15 on reasons for retweeting.
After forming the viral tweets dataset, duplicates were eliminated and an expert manually inspected tweet text to label fake news, producing the publicly available annotated dataset BIBREF8.
The paragraph introduces tweet fields returned by Twitter's API used to compare distributions between viral tweets containing fake news and viral tweets not containing fake news.

The next section graphically describes attribute distributions for the two tweet sets, normalizes or takes logarithms where appropriate, and uses the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test with a null hypothesis of equal distributions.

The sample contained 1 785 855 tweets from 848 196 different users, including 1327 viral tweets retweeted more than 1000 times by the 8th of November 2016, produced by 643 users and retweeted on 290 841 occasions.

A single person manually annotated the 1327 `viral' tweets, identifying 136 as potentially containing fake news, while noting ambiguity, human judgement, and that the dataset is not claimed as ground truth.
The following results detail tweet characteristics along previously mentioned dimensions, and Table TABREF23 reports actual differences and associated p-values for every variable considered.
Figure FIGREF24 shows viral tweets containing fake news were created more recently than other viral tweets, so Twitter users were exposed to election-related fake news for a shorter period.
Figure FIGREF25 shows no apparent retweet difference between tweets containing fake news or not, confirmed by the Kolmogorov-Smirnoff test not discarding equal associated distributions.
Users generating at least a viral tweet containing fake news appear to have, on average, less favourites, but Figure FIGREF26 visual differences are not statistically significant.
Viral fake news appears to use more hashtags than other viral tweets in Figure FIGREF27, but no statistical difference was found between average hashtags in viral tweets and viral fake news.

82 users spread fake news; 34 had verified accounts, 48 were unverified, 6 were suspended, 3 imitated legitimate accounts, 4 were deleted, and Figure FIGREF28 shows fake news more likely from unverified accounts.

Accounts distributing fake news appear to have, on average, the same number of friends as accounts distributing tweets with no fake news, but Figure FIGREF29 shows a statistically significant difference in distributions.

Accounts generating viral tweets with fake news have a very different follower distribution from accounts generating viral tweets with no fake news in Figure FIGREF30, with statistically significant differences.

Figures FIGREF31 and FIGREF32 show accounts spreading viral tweets with fake news have, on average, a larger friends/followers ratio, while accounts not generating fake news are more evenly distributed.
Figure FIGREF33 shows viral tweets labelled as containing fake news use mentions less frequently, mostly containing 1 mention versus two in other tweets, with statistically significant differences.
Figure FIGREF34 shows tweets labelled as not containing fake news appear to present more media elements than tweets labelled as fake news, but the difference is not statistically significant.

Figure FIGREF35 shows viral tweets containing fake news appear to include more URLs to other sites than viral tweets without fake news, with a statistically significant difference assuming INLINEFORM0.

Manual inspection of viral tweets labelled as containing fake news shows 117 expressed support for Donald Trump, 8 supported Hillary Clinton, and the remaining tweets concerned other topics without candidate support.
Constrained by the existing dataset, the authors introduce observations about differences between viral tweets labelled as containing fake news and viral tweets labelled as not containing them.

Findings related to Table TABREF44 suggest specific meta-data may identify fake news, especially time of exposure, shorter-lived viral fake-news tweets, deleted or suspended accounts, account lifetime, content age, and scrutiny of newly created accounts.

Accounts spreading fake news appear to have a larger friends/followers proportion, with the same average friends but fewer followers, and tweets containing fake news have more URLs, suggesting these features could single-out fake news.
Viral fake news content was highly polarized, in line with Alcott et al. BIBREF9, suggesting textual sentiment analysis together with meta-data parameters may help identify fake news.

The authors present a preliminary study on meta-data from a publicly available dataset of tweets that became viral during the day of the 2016 US presidential election, aiming to understand features of viral tweets containing fake news.

The authors argue automatic identification requires understanding and modelling deceitful tweets before tagging and blocking can succeed, anticipate spam-like evolution, and describe their meta-data angle as novel and complementary to content-focused works.

Within the used dataset, differences around exposure, characteristics of accounts spreading fake news, and tone of content suggest fake news can be modelled and automatically detected; the authors plan replication in an extended sample until 4 months after the US election.
No competing financial interest exist.
